claim: External and internal morphological characters of extant and fossil organisms are crucial to establishing their systematic position, ecological role and evolutionary trends.
source: External and internal morphological characters of extant and fossil organisms are crucial to establishing their systematic position, ecological role and evolutionary trends.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the importance of morphological characters in systematics and evolutionary biology.

claim: The lack of internal characters and soft-tissue preservation in many arthropod fossils impedes comprehensive phylogenetic analyses and species descriptions according to taxonomic standards for Recent organisms.
source: The lack of internal characters and soft-tissue preservation in many arthropod fossils, however, impedes comprehensive phylogenetic analyses and species descriptions according to taxonomic standards for Recent organisms.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about limitations in fossil preservation and their impact on phylogenetic studies.

claim: Well-preserved three-dimensional anatomy exists in mineralized arthropods from Paleogene fissure fillings.
source: We found well-preserved three-dimensional anatomy in mineralized arthropods from Paleogene fissure fillings and demonstrate the value of these fossils by utilizing digitally reconstructed anatomical structure of a hister beetle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' direct observations and data from X-ray microtomography of the fossil specimens.

claim: The new anatomical data facilitate a refinement of the species diagnosis of Onthophilus intermedius.
source: The new anatomical data facilitate a refinement of the species diagnosis and allowed us to reject a previous hypothesis of close phylogenetic relationship to an extant congeneric species.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed anatomical observations from microtomography and the extended species description provided in the manuscript.

claim: The previous hypothesis of close phylogenetic relationship between Onthophilus intermedius and O. striatus is rejected.
source: The new anatomical data facilitate a refinement of the species diagnosis and allowed us to reject a previous hypothesis of close phylogenetic relationship to an extant congeneric species.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis results showing these species in distinct clades.

claim: Mineralized fossils, even those of macroscopically poor preservation, constitute a rich but yet largely unexploited source of anatomical data for fossil arthropods.
source: Our findings suggest that mineralized fossils, even those of macroscopically poor preservation, constitute a rich but yet largely unexploited source of anatomical data for fossil arthropods.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that specimen F1994, which appeared poorly preserved externally, contained exceptional internal preservation.

claim: Internal characters play critical roles in ecomorphological and systematic studies.
source: While external characters predominate in ecomorphological and systematic studies, internal characters also play critical roles (Perreau and Tafforeau, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Internal characters in fossil specimens are usually not preserved or difficult to access.
source: In fossil specimens, however, these characters are usually not preserved or difficult to access (Siveter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge in paleontology.

claim: Combined phylogenetic analyses of extant species frequently utilize internal anatomy.
source: While combined phylogenetic analyses of extant species frequently utilize internal anatomy, analyses including fossil taxa are generally limited to external characters.
evidence: This represents established practice in phylogenetic systematics.

claim: Analyses including fossil taxa are generally limited to external characters.
source: While combined phylogenetic analyses of extant species frequently utilize internal anatomy, analyses including fossil taxa are generally limited to external characters.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about limitations in fossil-based phylogenetic analyses.

claim: It is often difficult to distinguish whether unobserved morphological characters were originally absent or lost due to taphonomic processes.
source: Moreover, it is often difficult to distinguish whether unobserved morphological characters were originally absent or lost due to taphonomic processes, potentially leading to misinterpretations of character evolution and erroneous phylogenetic placements (Sansom, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on taphonomic biases.

claim: Difficulty distinguishing absent from lost characters can potentially lead to misinterpretations of character evolution and erroneous phylogenetic placements.
source: Moreover, it is often difficult to distinguish whether unobserved morphological characters were originally absent or lost due to taphonomic processes, potentially leading to misinterpretations of character evolution and erroneous phylogenetic placements (Sansom, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents logical inference about the consequences of taphonomic uncertainty.

claim: Amber inclusions are famous for exquisitely preserving three-dimensional external shape and sometimes internal characters.
source: Amber inclusions are famous for exquisitely preserving three-dimensional external shape and sometimes internal characters (Perreau and Tafforeau, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about amber preservation.

claim: Three-dimensional arthropods may be preserved within concretions (e.g. in siderite nodules).
source: Three-dimensional arthropods may also be preserved within concretions (e.g. in siderite nodules [Nitecki, 1979; Garwood et al., 2009]), calcareous incrustations (e.g. in travertine [Rosendahl et al., 2013]), encapsulations in minerals (e.g. in onyx-marble [Pierce, 1951], chert [Anderson and Trewin, 2003], or gypsum crystals [Schlüter et al., 2003]), and mineral replications (e.g. as calcite [McCobb et al., 1998], silica [Miller and Lubkin, 2001], goethite [Grimaldi, 2009; Barling et al., 2014], pyrite [Grimaldi and Engel, 2005], or phosphate [Duncan and Briggs, 1996; Hellmund and Hellmund, 1996; Waloszek, 2003]).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work documenting these preservation types.

claim: Eyes have been reported in fossil insects.
source: For insects, e.g. eyes (Duncan and Briggs, 1996) and muscle fibers (Grimaldi, 2009) have been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Muscle fibers have been reported in fossil insects.
source: For insects, e.g. eyes (Duncan and Briggs, 1996) and muscle fibers (Grimaldi, 2009) have been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from the Oligocene fissure fillings of Ronheim.
source: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from the Oligocene fissure fillings of Ronheim (Hellmund and Hellmund, 1996), the Late Oligocene/Early Miocene limestones of Riversleigh (QLD, Australia) (Duncan and Briggs, 1996) and from Paleogene deposits at Quercy (south-central France) (Filhol, 1877; Gervais, 1877; Flach, 1890; Thévenin, 1903; Handschin, 1944).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from the Late Oligocene/Early Miocene limestones of Riversleigh (QLD, Australia).
source: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from the Oligocene fissure fillings of Ronheim (Hellmund and Hellmund, 1996), the Late Oligocene/Early Miocene limestones of Riversleigh (QLD, Australia) (Duncan and Briggs, 1996) and from Paleogene deposits at Quercy (south-central France) (Filhol, 1877; Gervais, 1877; Flach, 1890; Thévenin, 1903; Handschin, 1944).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from Paleogene deposits at Quercy (south-central France).
source: Abundant arthropod fossils preserved by mineralization of calcium phosphate are known from the Oligocene fissure fillings of Ronheim (Hellmund and Hellmund, 1996), the Late Oligocene/Early Miocene limestones of Riversleigh (QLD, Australia) (Duncan and Briggs, 1996) and from Paleogene deposits at Quercy (south-central France) (Filhol, 1877; Gervais, 1877; Flach, 1890; Thévenin, 1903; Handschin, 1944).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The Ronheim, Riversleigh, and Quercy localities have long been famous for their rich vertebrate fossils.
source: These localities have long been famous for their rich vertebrate fossils as well (e.g. Legendre et al., 1997; Laloy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The arthropod fossils of Quercy were documented by Swiss entomologist Eduard Handschin in 1944.
source: The arthropod fossils of Quercy were documented by Swiss entomologist Eduard Handschin (1944).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Handschin described the hister beetle Onthophilus intermedius (Coleoptera: Histeridae) from eight specimens.
source: He described the hister beetle Onthophilus intermedius (Coleoptera: Histeridae) from eight specimens, and considered it distinct but closely related to the extant European species O. striatus (Forster, 1771).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Handschin's work.

claim: Handschin considered Onthophilus intermedius distinct but closely related to the extant European species O. striatus.
source: He described the hister beetle Onthophilus intermedius (Coleoptera: Histeridae) from eight specimens, and considered it distinct but closely related to the extant European species O. striatus (Forster, 1771).
evidence: This is a historical fact about Handschin's hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: Handschin's description of Onthophilus intermedius was vague and based mainly on the external morphology of the two best-preserved specimens.
source: The description, however, was vague and based mainly on the external morphology of the two best-preserved specimens (Handschin, 1944).
evidence: This is an assessment of Handschin's work based on citation and the authors' evaluation.

claim: X-ray microtomography has become established for the detailed examination of both extant and extinct arthropods.
source: X-ray microtomography has become established for the detailed examination of both extant (e.g. Betz et al., 2007; Bosselaers et al., 2010; van de Kamp et al., 2011; 2014; 2015; Brehm et al., 2015; Sombke et al., 2015) and extinct (Sutton, 2008; Sutton et al., 2014) arthropods, including fossils preserved in amber (Lak et al., 2009; Pohl et al., 2010; Soriano et al., 2010; Perreau and Tafforeau, 2011; Riedel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting the use of this technique.

claim: Internal characters were found in all Onthophilus intermedius fossils examined.
source: We found internal characters in all fossils (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' direct observations from microtomography data, as documented in Table 1.

claim: Three specimens of Onthophilus intermedius show remains of inner organs, especially of the sclerotized genitalia.
source: Three specimens show remains of inner organs, especially of the sclerotized genitalia, allowing their identification as two males and one female.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from the microtomography data.

claim: Two male and one female specimens of Onthophilus intermedius were identified based on genital remains.
source: Three specimens show remains of inner organs, especially of the sclerotized genitalia, allowing their identification as two males and one female.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of sclerotized genitalia in the specimens.

claim: The outer surfaces of most Onthophilus intermedius specimens appear smooth.
source: The outer surfaces of most specimens appear smooth (Figure 2); the distinct punctuation found in extant Onthophilus species (Kovarik and Caterino, 2005) is faint.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimens and comparison with extant species.

claim: The distinct punctuation found in extant Onthophilus species is faint in the fossils.
source: The outer surfaces of most specimens appear smooth (Figure 2); the distinct punctuation found in extant Onthophilus species (Kovarik and Caterino, 2005) is faint.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with extant species, supported by citation.

claim: Specimen F1994 differs from all other samples by the presence of a stony matrix covering the ventral part of the beetle.
source: The specimen F1994 (Figures 1A,D,G, 2, 3, Supplementary file 1) differs from all other samples by the presence of a stony matrix, covering the ventral part of the beetle.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The dorsal part and head of specimen F1994 are exposed.
source: Its dorsal part and head are exposed; the elytra are missing and were probably detached before embedding.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The elytra of specimen F1994 were probably detached before embedding.
source: Its dorsal part and head are exposed; the elytra are missing and were probably detached before embedding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the elytra are missing.

claim: The exposed surface of specimen F1994 is partly eroded, especially in the anterior region of the head.
source: The exposed surface is partly eroded, especially in the anterior region of the head, and no appendages are visible from the outside.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: No appendages are visible from the outside of specimen F1994.
source: The exposed surface is partly eroded, especially in the anterior region of the head, and no appendages are visible from the outside.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The matrix of specimen F1994 concealed the best-preserved fossil from the collection.
source: The matrix, however, concealed the best-preserved fossil from the collection, which we examine here in detail.
evidence: This is based on the authors' comparative assessment of all specimens after microtomography.

claim: The ventral portion of specimen F1994 covered by the matrix reveals an extraordinary preservation of exoskeletal fine structures and internal anatomy.
source: The ventral portion of the beetle covered by the matrix reveals an extraordinary preservation of exoskeletal fine structures and internal anatomy (Figures 3, 4 and 5; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Some fractions of the cuticle in specimen F1994 appear to be mineralized.
source: While some fractions of the cuticle appear to be mineralized, the latter is mostly represented by air-filled spaces in the fossil (Figure 1A,D,G).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The cuticle in specimen F1994 is mostly represented by air-filled spaces in the fossil.
source: While some fractions of the cuticle appear to be mineralized, the latter is mostly represented by air-filled spaces in the fossil (Figure 1A,D,G).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The surface of the exoskeleton in specimen F1994 is preserved as a three-dimensional imprint of remarkable detail.
source: The surface of the exoskeleton is preserved as a three-dimensional imprint of remarkable detail; the body sclerites show characteristic punctuation of the genus.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The body sclerites of specimen F1994 show characteristic punctuation of the genus Onthophilus.
source: The surface of the exoskeleton is preserved as a three-dimensional imprint of remarkable detail; the body sclerites show characteristic punctuation of the genus.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data and comparison with known characteristics of the genus.

claim: The right foreleg of specimen F1994 is not preserved.
source: The right foreleg is not preserved; the left one is truncated from the trochanter; distal parts of the leg were lost prior to fossilization.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The left foreleg of specimen F1994 is truncated from the trochanter.
source: The right foreleg is not preserved; the left one is truncated from the trochanter; distal parts of the leg were lost prior to fossilization.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Distal parts of the left foreleg of specimen F1994 were lost prior to fossilization.
source: The right foreleg is not preserved; the left one is truncated from the trochanter; distal parts of the leg were lost prior to fossilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the leg is truncated.

claim: Large parts of the alimentary canal are visible inside specimen F1994.
source: Moreover, many anatomical characters can be recognized inside the fossil (Figure 3D). Apart from internal invaginations of the exoskeleton (e.g. tentorium, furcal arms and metendosternite), large parts of the alimentary canal and tracheal system are visible.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Large parts of the tracheal system are visible inside specimen F1994.
source: Moreover, many anatomical characters can be recognized inside the fossil (Figure 3D). Apart from internal invaginations of the exoskeleton (e.g. tentorium, furcal arms and metendosternite), large parts of the alimentary canal and tracheal system are visible.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The oesophagus in specimen F1994 appears to be shrunken and is connected to the crop.
source: The oesophagus appears to be shrunken and is connected to the crop, which is truncated posteriorly.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The crop in specimen F1994 is truncated posteriorly.
source: The oesophagus appears to be shrunken and is connected to the crop, which is truncated posteriorly.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The anterior part of the hindgut in specimen F1994 is hollow.
source: The anterior part of the hindgut is hollow, while the middle part is apparently filled with mineral matrix but well-defined.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The middle part of the hindgut in specimen F1994 is apparently filled with mineral matrix but well-defined.
source: The anterior part of the hindgut is hollow, while the middle part is apparently filled with mineral matrix but well-defined.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Conspicuous spherical particles in specimen F1994 may constitute remnants of gut content.
source: Conspicuous spherical particles may constitute remnants of gut content (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is speculative interpretation based on observation of spherical particles in the gut region.

claim: Some large tracheae in specimen F1994 appear to be filled with matrix, while others are hollow.
source: Like in the alimentary canal, some large tracheae appear to be filled with matrix, while others are hollow.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Most muscles in specimen F1994 can only be recognized by remnants at the insertion areas.
source: Except for the musculature connecting the right pro- and mesofurcal arms (Figure 1D), most muscles can only be recognized by remnants at the insertion areas (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The genitals in specimen F1994 are extraordinary well-preserved.
source: The genitals are extraordinary well-preserved (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: Testes and Ductus ejaculatorius could not be recognized in specimen F1994.
source: While testes and Ductus ejaculatorius could not be recognized, other soft tissues such as the spiral accessory glands and parts of the gland ducts are conspicuous.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The spiral accessory glands and parts of the gland ducts are conspicuous in specimen F1994.
source: While testes and Ductus ejaculatorius could not be recognized, other soft tissues such as the spiral accessory glands and parts of the gland ducts are conspicuous.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The genital sclerites in specimen F1994, including aedeagus, median lobe, gonopore, tergites 8-10 and sternites 8 & 9, are almost perfectly preserved as imprints.
source: The genital sclerites, including aedeagus, median lobe, gonopore, tergites 8-10 and sternites 8 & 9 are almost perfectly preserved as imprints.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography data.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis resulted in 72 most parsimonious trees of length 185 (CI 0.27, RI 0.61).
source: The analysis resulted in 72 most parsimonious trees of length 185 (CI 0.27, RI 0.61).
evidence: This is the direct result of the phylogenetic analysis performed.

claim: Onthophilus intermedius is part of a trichotomy involving O. silvae and a large group of species descended from the common ancestor of O. giganteus and O. niponensis.
source: O. intermedius is part of a trichotomy involving O. silvae Lewis, 1884 and a large group of species descended from the common ancestor of O. giganteus Heleva, 1978 and O. niponensis, though in reweighted trees it is resolved as sister to O. silvae alone.
evidence: This is based on the results of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In reweighted trees, Onthophilus intermedius is resolved as sister to O. silvae alone.
source: O. intermedius is part of a trichotomy involving O. silvae Lewis, 1884 and a large group of species descended from the common ancestor of O. giganteus Heleva, 1978 and O. niponensis, though in reweighted trees it is resolved as sister to O. silvae alone.
evidence: This is based on the results of the phylogenetic analysis with character reweighting.

claim: In all analyses, O. striatus is nested within a lineage of Nearctic and far-eastern Palaearctic species.
source: In all analyses O. striatus is nested within a lineage of Nearctic and far-eastern Palaearctic species, including O. flavicornis Lewis, 1884, O. flohri Lewis, 1888 and others.
evidence: This is based on the results of all phylogenetic analyses performed.

claim: There are seven characters by which the states of O. intermedius and O. striatus differ, three external and four internal.
source: Of the characters scored for both O. intermedius and O. striatus, there are seven by which their states differ, three external and four internal.
evidence: This is based on the character matrix compiled for the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Two external characters (29 & 30) and one internal character (36) are reconstructed as autapomorphies distinguishing O. intermedius and O. striatus.
source: Of these, two external (chars. 29 & 30) and one internal (char. 36) are reconstructed as autapomorphies (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on character mapping on the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Only one external synapomorphy (char. 22) separates O. intermedius and O. striatus.
source: Only one external synapomorphy (char. 22) separates them, while three of the four genitalic differences (chars. 35, 40, and 41) represent synapomorphies of their respective lineages.
evidence: This is based on character mapping on the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Three of the four genitalic differences (chars. 35, 40, and 41) between O. intermedius and O. striatus represent synapomorphies of their respective lineages.
source: Only one external synapomorphy (char. 22) separates them, while three of the four genitalic differences (chars. 35, 40, and 41) represent synapomorphies of their respective lineages.
evidence: This is based on character mapping on the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Exclusion of internal characters for O. intermedius did not affect the phylogenetic topology.
source: Exclusion of internal characters for O. intermedius did not affect the topology, but did prevent genitalic characters from supporting its larger containing clade.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the phylogenetic data.

claim: Exclusion of internal characters for O. intermedius prevented genitalic characters from supporting its larger containing clade.
source: Exclusion of internal characters for O. intermedius did not affect the topology, but did prevent genitalic characters from supporting its larger containing clade.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the phylogenetic data.

claim: Critical diagnostic differences in external morphology, such as mesoventral proportions and pygidial sculpturing, were revealed by visualization of features previously obscured by matrix.
source: Critical diagnostic differences in external morphology, such as mesoventral proportions and pygidial sculpturing, were also revealed by visualization of features previously obscured by matrix.
evidence: This is based on comparison of features visible in microtomography versus external examination.

claim: An accurate three-dimensional conservation of soft tissues does not occur if the specimens are dried in air.
source: An accurate three-dimensional conservation of soft tissues does not occur if the specimens are dried in air (Figure 1C,F,I).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the fossil with air-dried extant specimens.

claim: The fixation process must have occurred fast, possibly due to the animal being immediately penetrated and enclosed by phosphate rich water.
source: Therefore, the fixation process must have occurred fast, possibly due to the animal being immediately penetrated and enclosed by phosphate rich water.
evidence: This is inferred from the quality of soft tissue preservation and knowledge of fossilization processes.

claim: Replication of soft tissues by phosphatization may be accomplished over a period of weeks.
source: Replication of soft tissues by phosphatization may be accomplished over a period of weeks (Martı́nez-Delclòs et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on phosphatization processes.

claim: Possible sources for high phosphorous concentrations in water circulating through the fissure fill are rocks or abundant phosphate-rich vertebrate bones.
source: Possible sources for high phosphorous concentrations in water circulating through the fissure fill are rocks or abundant phosphate-rich vertebrate bones, which may have been deposited along with them (Handschin, 1944; Hellmund and Hellmund, 1996).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations about the depositional context.

claim: After encrustation and internal mineralization, the cuticle largely decayed, leaving air-filled spaces.
source: After encrustation and internal mineralization, the cuticle largely decayed, leaving air-filled spaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of air-filled spaces where cuticle should be and knowledge of fossilization processes.

claim: Erosion processes probably removed the outer stony matrix of most specimens, including fragile appendages and the imprint of the outer surface of the exoskeleton.
source: Erosion processes probably removed the outer stony matrix of most specimens, including fragile appendages and the imprint of the outer surface of the exoskeleton, leaving a mineralized endocast.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most specimens lack external matrix and appendages.

claim: The exterior of the fossils merely represents the inner surface of the exoskeleton.
source: Thus, the exterior of the fossils merely represents the inner surface of the exoskeleton – the deep grooves (Figure 2) actually being inner folds or apophyses.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the fossils with the detailed preservation in F1994.

claim: The deep grooves visible on most fossils are actually inner folds or apophyses.
source: Thus, the exterior of the fossils merely represents the inner surface of the exoskeleton – the deep grooves (Figure 2) actually being inner folds or apophyses.
evidence: This is inferred from understanding that the fossils represent endocasts.

claim: The smooth dorsal part of F1994 resembles the other fossils in appearance.
source: While the smooth dorsal part of F1994 resembles the other fossils in appearance, its ventral surface covered by the mineral matrix shows a distinct surface sculpturing as present in extant species of the genus.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison of specimens.

claim: The ventral surface of F1994 covered by the mineral matrix shows a distinct surface sculpturing as present in extant species of the genus.
source: While the smooth dorsal part of F1994 resembles the other fossils in appearance, its ventral surface covered by the mineral matrix shows a distinct surface sculpturing as present in extant species of the genus.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microtomography and comparison with extant species.

claim: An artificial 'digital endocast' created from the tomographic data of F1994 bears a striking resemblance to the other fossils.
source: In contrast, an artificial 'digital endocast' created from the tomographic data of F1994 (Material and methods) bears a striking resemblance to the other fossils (Figure 5), on which Handschin based his original description.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the digital endocast with other specimens.

claim: Handschin based his original description on fossils that were actually endocasts.
source: In contrast, an artificial 'digital endocast' created from the tomographic data of F1994 (Material and methods) bears a striking resemblance to the other fossils (Figure 5), on which Handschin based his original description.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the digital endocast resembles the fossils Handschin examined.

claim: The Quercy hister beetles represent three-dimensional 'hybrid' fossils, comprising cuticle imprints and mineralized soft tissue.
source: Summing up, the Quercy hister beetles represent three-dimensional 'hybrid' fossils, comprising cuticle imprints and mineralized soft tissue, combining to preserve both exoskeletal fine structure and internal anatomical characters.
evidence: This is a synthesis of observations about the preservation mode.

claim: The Quercy hister beetles combine preservation of both exoskeletal fine structure and internal anatomical characters.
source: Summing up, the Quercy hister beetles represent three-dimensional 'hybrid' fossils, comprising cuticle imprints and mineralized soft tissue, combining to preserve both exoskeletal fine structure and internal anatomical characters.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from microtomography.

claim: Fissure filling fossils preserving three-dimensional internal anatomy will help to overcome taphonomic biases in available fossil data.
source: Fissure filling fossils preserving three-dimensional internal anatomy will help to overcome taphonomic biases in available fossil data (Allison and Bottjer, 2011).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the future value of these fossils, supported by citation about taphonomic biases.

claim: Fossilized insect internal character information has mainly been obtained from well-preserved amber inclusions to date.
source: To date, fossilized insect internal character information has mainly been obtained from well-preserved amber inclusions (e.g. Pohl, et al., 2010; Perreau and Tafforeau, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a summary of the state of the field.

claim: The origination of amber as tree resin causes a representational bias toward generally arboreal taxa.
source: However, the origination of amber as tree resin causes a representational bias toward generally arboreal taxa (Martı́nez-Delclòs et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about amber taphonomy.

claim: The fossil arthropods of Quercy represent an assemblage of taxa more typically associated with forest floor communities.
source: The fossil arthropods of Quercy represent an assemblage of taxa more typically associated with forest floor communities (Handschin, 1944), as exemplified by Onthophilus, typically a predator in various decaying organic materials (Kovarik and Caterino, 2005; Bajerlein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations about the Quercy fauna and the ecology of Onthophilus.

claim: Onthophilus is typically a predator in various decaying organic materials.
source: The fossil arthropods of Quercy represent an assemblage of taxa more typically associated with forest floor communities (Handschin, 1944), as exemplified by Onthophilus, typically a predator in various decaying organic materials (Kovarik and Caterino, 2005; Bajerlein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations about the ecology of Onthophilus.

claim: Forest floor communities are less commonly preserved than those of many other environments.
source: Such communities are less commonly preserved than those of many other environments (Kidwell and Flessa, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation about taphonomic biases.

claim: Clearer interpretations of evolutionary relationships of these fossils will improve inferences about the evolution of these ecological communities.
source: Beyond anatomical data on these species, clearer interpretations of evolutionary relationships of these fossils will improve inferences about the evolution of these ecological communities.
evidence: This is logical inference about the value of phylogenetic information for understanding community evolution.

claim: Reexamination of the Quercy fossils may provide a highly complementary source of information on the evolutionary history of arthropods.
source: Thus, reexamination of the Quercy fossils, and likely also of similar mineralized fossils from other localities (which may represent different ecosystems and/or time periods), may provide a highly complementary source of information on the evolutionary history of arthropods.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study.

claim: Similar mineralized fossils from other localities may represent different ecosystems and/or time periods.
source: Thus, reexamination of the Quercy fossils, and likely also of similar mineralized fossils from other localities (which may represent different ecosystems and/or time periods), may provide a highly complementary source of information on the evolutionary history of arthropods.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential of other fossil localities.

claim: A fast tomography setup combining filtered polychromatic radiation and an optimized detector system is well-suited to achieve sufficient image quality in most fossil specimens.
source: Based on our experience, a fast tomography setup combining filtered polychromatic radiation and an optimized detector system (dos Santos Rolo et al., 2014) is well-suited to achieve sufficient image quality in most fossil specimens.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience with the technique and supported by citation.

claim: Scan duration per tomogram may be reduced to a couple of seconds, facilitating high-throughput screening of large sample numbers in short time.
source: Thus, scan duration per tomogram may be reduced to a couple of seconds (Material and methods), facilitating high-throughput screening of large sample numbers in short time.
evidence: This is based on the actual scan parameters used in the study.
